name: Bilal Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. Could you walk me through an ordinary shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead an underground cutting crew at a large potash mine and operate the continuous miner, the machine that cuts ore from the face. I check the roof, guide the cutter and listen for a change in the motor load before a jam. My two-year technical diploma helps with the controls, but teaching an apprentice to notice loose ground takes time beside the machine. My wife Farah runs a small pharmacy, and our two children are in school. We carry a mortgage but have eleven months of expenses saved. I use AI every day to compare cutter vibration notes, then check the machine myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew our cutter already makes more useful data than we read, so a quicker note tool is welcome. I would still make the person who checked the roof sign the shift book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my lead wage is safe in this picture, and Farah's pharmacy can cover some bills if the mine has a short shutdown. The mortgage stays on my mind, but eleven months saved keeps it from running my day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the roof walk and have the apprentice mark motor changes in the shift book. In the first year I'll use my AI note tool to sort vibration readings, then compare every flagged change with the cutter's service record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel comfortable with a tool that clears the clutter. I don't want an apprentice learning to trust a coloured box before learning the sound of a jam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did the tool misread the cutter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once the software called a normal start-up vibration a fault, and I checked the service record before stopping the cutter. That sort of false alarm is why I still ask who made the call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the household change its spending?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Farah our usual mortgage payment stays, and the children can keep their school trips. A small time saving doesn't call for a new machine purchase at home.

say: I would welcome **quicker notes** while keeping a named person responsible for the roof check.
I would tell apprentices to learn **motor sounds** before relying on coloured warnings.
think: I expect my **lead wage** to stay safe with modest changes to notes.
I can manage a short shutdown with **eleven months saved** and Farah’s pharmacy income.
do: **Keep the roof walk** and have apprentices record motor changes in the shift book.
**Compare AI vibration flags** with cutter service records during the first year.
feel: **Comfortable** with quicker notes, while protective of hands-on learning.
S0.quote: I would still make the person who checked the roof sign the shift book.
fieldNote: He uses **AI daily** but ties each roof decision to a named worker who saw the ground.
The **strong cushion** and second household income keep routine note automation from threatening his living.

steps.text: Keep checking the mine roof with apprentices before cutting
Compare AI vibration flags with cutter service records

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say planning, stores and shift reports will move to software first; robots will take longer to reach the cutting face. Give good operators access to the new data and let them challenge it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the mine may run fewer planning desks and ask my crew to cut more metres in a shift. My wage should hold, but a higher target could make someone skip a roof pause.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask for access to the planning tool and try it against three old cutting maps this month. In the first year I'll bring any false roof-clear marks to the foreman and propose a crew sign-off before the plan reaches the cutter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am keen to see the tool, yet uneasy about a target becoming a reason to hurry underground. A saved minute is worthless if the roof comes down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop a software plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the plan routes us beneath the old service tunnel, I would stop and check the support record. The cutter can wait while we find out whether the roof is sound.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach a new operator?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would teach the apprentice to compare the machine record and the face, not just copy my answer. I was trusted with a machine only after someone let me make a careful call.

say: I would expect **planning desks** to change before robots work at the cutting face.
I would give operators **data access** and a way to challenge a roof-clear mark.
think: I expect my **wage** to hold, though faster metre targets may pressure roof checks.
I worry that **rushed pauses** could hurt a worker before any robot arrives.
do: **Test the planning tool** this month against three previous cutting maps.
**Propose crew sign-off** for roof-clear marks during the first year.
feel: **Keen** to test the tool, but uneasy about time pressure underground.
S1.quote: A saved minute is worthless if the roof comes down.
fieldNote: He welcomes **planning software** as data to test, not a replacement for roof checks.
His **income feels secure**; concern centres on higher targets and safety for the crew.

steps.text: Test planning software against three old cutting maps
Keep crew roof sign-off before the cutter follows a plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew full thinking AI by 2028 could rewrite plans and stores orders, while capable cutting robots follow around 2031. We need a plan for apprentices before the machines can learn the whole face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my lead post could be smaller once robots cut and check the roof as well as us. Our savings buy a year, not another career, and the mortgage would still come each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this winter I'll use part of my bonus to take a certified machine-controls course with real equipment practice. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'll apply for a paid controls trainer post if one opens at a wage close to my current pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing the cutting roster, but I can start preparing now. I am more worried that apprentices will be told to learn a machine with no supervised hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you fund the controls course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Farah the course fee before I pay it, and keep our emergency fund untouched. Her pharmacy income is a backstop, not a reason to empty our own savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a trainer post real work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the mine whether a trainer can stop a machine from the control room and walk to the face afterward. A job title without that authority would not suit me.

say: I would distinguish **2028 planning AI** from capable cutting robots around 2031.
I would demand **supervised hours** for apprentices before equipment work shifts away from people.
think: I could lose part of my **cutting roster** once robots cut and inspect the roof.
I think our **eleven-month cushion** buys time, but the mortgage still needs an income.
do: **Fund certified controls training** from my bonus this winter, with real equipment practice.
**Apply** for a paid trainer post after thinking AI arrives if an opening offers near-current pay and real stop authority.
feel: **Anxious** about his roster, with money to train and a conditional job path.
S2.quote: Our savings buy a year, not another career, and the mortgage would still come each month.
fieldNote: He identifies **2031 cutting robots** as the direct threat; 2028 thinking AI changes plans and stores first.
His **trainer application** depends on an opening, near-current pay and meaningful control authority; the course fee comes from a bonus.

steps.text: Pay for certified controls training with bonus money and real equipment practice
Apply for an open paid trainer post if wage stays close and stop authority is granted

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say full thinking AI by 2031 and capable robots around 2034 give us time to test new cutters properly. I would like the mine to publish separate pay rates for operators, maintainers and trainers before anyone applies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 51 when cutting robots arrive, and I could see myself teaching controls if the role is truly paid as skilled work. There are other mines nearby. I would not move my children for a mine trainer title without a written job offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll spend a few Saturdays this year training apprentices on the current cutter and record what goes wrong in practice. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'll apply for a posted controls trainer role if the wage, supervised hours and stop authority are written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel interested in the chance to teach, with some worry about the wage. Five years gives me time to test what a new role really entails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you reject a trainer opening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the posted wage is lower than our mortgage plan allows, I will stay on the cutting roster while it lasts. I can look at other nearby mines without moving the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your wife need to see in an offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show Farah the posted pay sheet and work hours before saying yes. Pharmacy shifts and school pickup need a real timetable, not a promise.

say: I would use the **five-year window** to test cutters before capable robots arrive around 2034.
I would ask for **published pay** across operating, maintenance and trainer posts.
think: I think at **51**, I could teach controls if the job pays for skilled work.
I would keep my **children settled** rather than move for an unoffered title.
do: **Train apprentices** on the current cutter during several Saturdays this year.
**Apply** for a posted trainer role after thinking AI arrives only with written pay, supervised hours and stop authority.
feel: **Interested** in teaching, with concern about whether a trainer wage will support the mortgage.
S3.quote: I would not move my children for a mine trainer title without a written job offer.
fieldNote: He calculates **2034 robot arrival** at 51 and sees teaching controls as a related role.
His **application** depends on a posted job with written pay, hours and stop authority; nearby mines provide another option.

steps.text: Train apprentices on the current cutting machine this year
Apply for a posted controls trainer role if pay and authority are written

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the thinking work changes in 2036 and capable cutting robots arrive around 2039. A decade is enough for the mine to build a proper apprenticeship route instead of a quick online badge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 56 when robots arrive and could have most of the mortgage paid if we keep the current plan. I might reduce cutting shifts then, but only if Farah's shop and my retirement figures support it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep leading the cutting shift and making scheduled mortgage payments, then review retirement figures with Farah each year. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'll compare a posted trainer role with my retirement estimate before deciding whether to reduce shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our household with a decade to prepare. I would miss the cutting face, but I could still be useful teaching a new crew if a job exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you keep full shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the pharmacy has a bad year, I would keep full mine shifts while they're offered. I would not ask our children to trade school plans for my early exit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What advice would you give the apprentices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the apprentices to keep learning the rock as well as the controls. A machine can change, but a careful worker can carry judgment to the next one.

say: I would use the **decade** to build practical apprenticeships before cutting robots around 2039.
I would keep **rock judgment** beside new controls for younger operators.
think: I think at **56**, I might reduce shifts if the mortgage falls and the pharmacy stays sound.
I want **retirement figures** before deciding whether a trainer role is worth taking.
do: **Keep leading** cutting shifts, make scheduled mortgage payments and review retirement figures with Farah each year.
**Compare a posted role** with retirement figures after thinking AI arrives before reducing cutting shifts.
feel: **Calm** about household finances, with some sadness about leaving the cutting face.
S4.quote: A machine can change, but a careful worker can carry judgment to the next one.
fieldNote: His **2039 age** is 56, so fewer shifts are possible if mortgage progress and pharmacy income hold.
He makes **no early retirement commitment** before seeing retirement figures and a posted trainer role.

steps.text: Keep leading cutting shifts and making scheduled mortgage payments
Compare a posted trainer role with retirement figures after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable cutting robots could arrive around 2031 before apprentices have supervised practice. A certified course with real machines and a paid trainer opening would help me prepare without spending our emergency fund.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who takes responsibility when a roof check comes from a remote control room. A remote roof check still needs a named operator who can stop the cutter. I would want that operator to walk to the face afterward.

headlineQuote: A remote roof check still needs a named operator who can stop the cutter.
portrait: **Bilal Tanaka**, 43, leads an underground cutting crew at a large potash mine and holds a two-year technical diploma.
He uses **AI daily** for vibration notes but checks the roof and cutting machine himself before trusting a warning.
His **higher mine wage**, eleven months of savings and his wife’s pharmacy support two children and a mortgage.
He will fund **controls training** from a bonus and consider a trainer post only with written pay and authority.
He favours **practical apprenticeships** and household self-reliance while using new tools earlier than most colleagues.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because cutting robots could arrive around 2031 before apprentices gain supervised hours.
whatWouldHelp: A **certified practical course** and a paid trainer opening would let him prepare without spending emergency savings.
